mainTopic: Responsibility for damage in someone else's חצר: permission, accepting guarding, and רב's rule that 'it should not have eaten'
overview: The amud finishes the משנה about bringing an ox into a homeowner's חצר. Without permission, the homeowner is פטור for harm done to the ox, and the ox's owner pays for damage it causes. With permission, the בעל החצר is responsible, while רבי says no one is liable unless he clearly agreed to guard. The גמרא finds that the משנה seems to switch between רבי and the רבנן. רבי זירא says different clauses come from different teachers. רבא says the opening is all רבנן, because permission puts guarding only on the בעל החצר. Next, רב rules that a produce owner pays only if the animal slipped on the produce, not if it ate it, since 'it should not have eaten.' The גמרא defends רב against three ברייתות: the poison case, the woman grinding wheat, and the ox that ate wheat and died. Finally it asks whether accepting guarding also covers damage from outside, and tests this with a ברייתא about an outside ox eating produce. That discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: An ox brought in without permission: who pays for goring?
steps.stepSummary: Someone brought his ox into a חצר without permission. If the homeowner's ox or dog hurts it, the homeowner is פטור. If it gores the homeowner's ox, its owner is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he brought his ox in without permission and the homeowner's ox gored it, or the homeowner's dog bit it, the homeowner is exempt. If his ox gored the homeowner's ox, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues its case of an ox brought into another person's חצר without permission and rules on goring in both directions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the ox came in without permission, the homeowner owes nothing for harm done to it on his property. But the trespassing ox's owner still pays for any damage his ox does there.

phrases.aramaic: בִּרְשׁוּת, וּנְגָחוֹ שׁוֹרוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת,
phrases.english: [without] permission, and the homeowner's ox gored it,
phrases.notes: This sentence started just before this section: a man brought his ox into someone's חצר without permission.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁנְּשָׁכוֹ כַּלְבּוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: or the homeowner's dog bit it – he is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: נָגַח הוּא שׁוֹרוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: If it gored the homeowner's ox – he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's case from before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without permission: the homeowner is פטור for harm to the visiting ox, and the visiting ox's owner is חייב for harm it causes.

steps.title: The ox falls into the homeowner's pit
steps.stepSummary: If the trespassing ox falls into the homeowner's בור and spoils the water, its owner is חייב. If the homeowner's father or son was in the pit, he pays כופר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it fell into his pit and made the water stink, he is liable. If his father or son was inside the pit, he pays the ransom.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds more cases where the trespassing ox causes damage. This time the ox falls into the homeowner's pit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the owner of a pit pays when an animal falls in. Here the ox did not belong there, so its owner pays instead, both for spoiling the water and כופר if a person in the pit was killed.

keyTerms.meaning: a pit, here one that holds water
ransom payment owed when an ox kills a person

steps.confusionAlert: Here the owner of the ox that fell in is the one who pays. The pit owner does not pay, because the ox came in without permission.

phrases.english: If it fell into his pit and spoiled its water – he is liable.
If his father or his son was inside it –
phrases.notes: The homeowner's relative was in the pit and died when the ox fell on him.

phrases.english: he pays the ransom.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more damages caused by the same trespassing ox.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The trespassing ox's owner pays for spoiled water, and pays כופר if a person in the pit is killed.

steps.title: With permission, the courtyard owner is responsible
steps.stepSummary: If the ox was brought in with permission, the בעל החצר is חייב for the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he brought it in with permission, the owner of the courtyard is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה turns to the opposite case: the ox came in with permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the first opinion (the תנא קמא), giving permission means the courtyard owner took responsibility for what happens in his yard. So he is liable for damage done there.

phrases.english: But if he brought it in with permission –
the owner of the courtyard is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposite case: with permission instead of without.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When permission is given, the בעל החצר is responsible for the damage.

steps.title: רבי: no one is liable without agreeing to guard
steps.stepSummary: רבי says that in all these cases the homeowner is not liable unless he clearly agreed to guard.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי says: In all of them he is not liable until he takes it upon himself to guard.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי disagrees with the first opinion about the permission case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי, permission alone is not enough to create responsibility. Only an explicit agreement to guard makes the courtyard owner liable.
steps.whatToRemember: The two opinions differ on one point. תנא קמא holds that permission brings responsibility with it. רבי holds that only an explicit promise to guard creates responsibility.

phrases.english: Rabbi says:
In all of them he is not liable,
until he accepts upon himself to guard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the permission ruling in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no liability unless one explicitly agrees to guard.

steps.title: An inference from the pots case: whose view is it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the first case of the משנה (pots brought in without permission) to show that with permission the potter would not pay for harm to the owner's animal. Then it asks whose view that is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that it was without permission. So if it was with permission, the pot owner is not liable for injuries to the courtyard owner's animal. We do not say the pot owner took on the job of guarding the courtyard owner's animal. Whose view is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from the משנה's opening case and then asks which תנא holds it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The potter pays only because he came in without permission. So with permission he would not pay, which means we do not assume he agreed to guard the owner's animal. That fits poorly with the תנא קמא, who reads responsibility into permission, so the גמרא asks whose view this is.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The reason is that it was without permission,
but with permission –
the owner of the pots would not be liable
for injuries to the courtyard owner's animal,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אָמְרִינַן קַבּוֹלֵי קַבֵּיל בַּעַל קְדֵירוֹת
phrases.english: and we do not say that the pot owner accepted
the guarding of the courtyard owner's animal;
Whose view is this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא begins analyzing the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that permission alone does not make the potter responsible for guarding the owner's animal?

steps.title: It is רבי's view
steps.stepSummary: The inference follows רבי: when permission is given without details, nobody has taken on guarding.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבי, who says: whenever it is unspecified, he has not taken guarding upon himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. The opening case of the משנה follows רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's rule works in both directions. The courtyard owner does not guard the guest's items, and the guest does not guard the owner's animal, unless someone says so clearly.
steps.whatToRemember: The first case of the משנה follows רבי: plain permission never means a promise to guard, for either side.

phrases.english: It is Rabbi, who says:
Whenever it is unspecified –
he did not accept upon himself guarding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The inference follows רבי, who holds that plain permission does not create any duty to guard.

steps.title: The next clause seems to follow the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: The clause 'if he brought them in with permission, the בעל החצר is liable' matches the רבנן, who hold that unspecified permission includes taking on guarding.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look at the next clause: if the potter brought the pots in with permission, the owner of the courtyard is liable. Here we have reached the view of the רבנן, who say that even when permission is given without details, the owner takes on the job of guarding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the next clause of the משנה and shows that it follows the רבנן, not רבי. This is the start of a problem: the first clause followed רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 6 the first clause was explained by רבי's view: plain permission does not include guarding. But this clause makes the בעל החצר liable just because he gave permission. That only works if plain permission does include guarding, which is the view of the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: We have arrived at the view of the רבנן
Without details, with no specific terms stated

phrases.english: Say the next clause:
If he brought them in with permission,
the owner of the courtyard is liable.
We have arrived at the רבנן, who say:
phrases.notes: These are the חכמים who disagree with רבי at the end of the משנה.

phrases.english: even with plain, unspecified permission,
he accepts upon himself the guarding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the clause right after the one explained in step 6 follows the opposite view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 6 that the משנה follows רבי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The next clause makes plain permission include guarding, which is the רבנן's view, so the משנה cannot be all רבי.

steps.title: The last line is רבי again, so the משנה switches back and forth
steps.stepSummary: The end of the משנה states רבי's view outright, so the first and last parts are רבי and the middle part is רבנן, which seems very unlikely.
steps.simpleTranslation: And more than that: the משנה ends, 'רבי says: in all these cases he is not liable unless the homeowner agrees to guard.' So the first clause and the last clause are רבי, and the middle clause is the רבנן?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds to the problem by pointing to the end of the משנה, which is plainly רבי. Now the משנה looks like it goes רבי, then רבנן, then רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the problem was two clauses next to each other that disagree. Now it is worse, because a רבנן clause sits between two רבי clauses. A משנה is not expected to jump between opinions like that, so the גמרא asks how this can be.

phrases.english: And furthermore, רבי says:
in all of them he is not liable,

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיְּקַבֵּל עָלָיו בַּעַל הַבַּיִת לִשְׁמוֹר.
phrases.english: unless the homeowner accepts upon himself to guard.
So the first and last clauses are רבי,
and the middle clause is the רבנן?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Makes the challenge of step 7 sharper by showing the משנה goes back to רבי at the end.
steps.kashyaTarget: The way the משנה is being read
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A single משנה should not go רבי, רבנן, רבי; this reading seems impossible.

steps.title: רבי זירא: different parts were taught by different תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא accepts that the משנה is split: whoever taught one clause did not teach the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: Break it apart. The one who taught this clause did not teach that clause.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers the problem by agreeing that the משנה does not follow one view. He says the clauses come from different teachers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not try to make the משנה fit one opinion. Instead he accepts the switching: the first and last clauses are רבי, and the middle is the רבנן. This solves the problem by giving up on the משנה being one unified teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: Break it, the משנה is split apart

keyTerms.term: מִי שֶׁשָּׁנָה זוֹ לֹא שָׁנָה זוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: Whoever taught this did not teach that

phrases.english: רבי זירא said: Break it apart;
phrases.notes: Literally 'break it.' He means the משנה is not one piece.

phrases.english: whoever taught this clause
did not teach that clause.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8 by accepting that the משנה is split.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the משנה between different תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole משנה must follow one opinion.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clauses come from different teachers, so switching views is fine.

steps.title: רבא: the whole first section follows the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the first clause is also רבנן: with permission, the בעל החצר took on guarding the pots, but the potter took on nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is all the רבנן. When permission was given, the owner of the courtyard took on guarding the pots, even if they broke in the wind.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different answer: the first clause does not have to be רבי at all. It fits the רבנן too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן say plain permission means the בעל החצר takes on guarding the pots, so strongly that he pays even if wind breaks them. But that guarding goes one way only: the potter took on no duty to guard the owner's animals. So with permission the potter is not liable even according to the רבנן, and the inference from step 5 fits them.

keyTerms.meaning: It is all the view of the רבנן

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the רבנן say permission makes both sides responsible. For them, permission makes the בעל החצר guard the pots. It does not make the potter guard the owner's animals.
steps.whatToRemember: Two answers: רבי זירא says the משנה is split between רבי and the רבנן. רבא says the first section is all רבנן, because permission puts guarding only on the בעל החצר.

phrases.english: רבא said: It is all the רבנן,
and when there was permission,

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמִירַת קְדֵירוֹת קִבֵּל עָלָיו בַּעַל הֶחָצֵר,
phrases.english: the owner of the courtyard took upon himself guarding the pots,
even if they broke in the wind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another answer to step 8, instead of רבי זירא's split.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the first clause so it fits the רבנן
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first clause showed that permission puts no guarding on anyone, which only רבי holds.
steps.terutzMaskana: Permission puts guarding of the pots on the בעל החצר but puts nothing on the potter, so the first clause fits the רבנן too.

steps.title: רב: liable only when the animal slipped, not when it ate
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's produce case, רב says the produce owner is liable only if the animal slipped on the produce. If it ate the produce and got hurt, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If he brought his produce into the homeowner's courtyard, etc.' רב said: They taught this only when the animal slipped on the produce. But if it ate it, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next case in the משנה, produce brought in without permission. רב limits when the produce owner pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the produce owner pays if the homeowner's animal is hurt. רב narrows this to slipping. If the animal was hurt by eating the produce, the owner does not pay.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only in a case of

phrases.aramaic: הִכְנִיס פֵּירוֹתָיו לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: If he brought his produce into the homeowner's courtyard, etc.
רב said: They taught this only
where the animal slipped on them,
but if it ate them, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the pots case and starts the produce case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The produce owner pays only when the animal slipped on the produce, not when it ate it.

steps.title: Why is he exempt when the animal ate?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב's exemption.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב exempts the produce owner when the animal ate. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Either way the produce was in the courtyard without permission, so the difference between slipping and eating needs a reason.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רב's ruling in step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the produce owner is exempt when the animal ate the produce.

steps.title: The animal should not have eaten
steps.stepSummary: The animal is to blame for eating the produce, so the produce owner does not pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: The animal should not have eaten it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the animal did something it should not have done by eating. So the harm is on the animal, not the produce owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Slipping just happens to an animal walking, so the produce owner is at fault for leaving it there. Eating is the animal's own choice, so the produce owner is not to blame.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: a produce owner pays if the animal slipped on his produce, but not if it ate it, because the animal should not have eaten.

phrases.english: It should not have eaten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The animal was at fault for eating, so the produce owner is exempt.

steps.title: רב ששת challenges רב from the poison ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת says רב must have said his ruling while half-asleep. A ברייתא implies that putting edible produce before an animal makes you liable even in human court, which goes against רב's 'it should not have eaten' reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: I say that רב said this ruling while dozing and lying down. For a ברייתא teaches: One who puts poison in front of his friend's animal is exempt in human court but liable in the laws of Heaven. Only poison, which an animal does not usually eat, gets this exemption. But produce, which an animal usually eats, would make him liable in human court too! And why? The animal should not have eaten it!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת attacks רב's ruling from Step 11. He brings a ברייתא that seems to make a person liable when an animal eats his produce and is harmed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא exempts the person only in the case of poison, which animals do not normally eat. That suggests that with normal produce, which animals do eat, he would be liable in human court. But רב said that even with produce the animal is to blame for eating it, so the ברייתא seems to contradict רב.

keyTerms.meaning: While dozing and lying down: said without full attention

keyTerms.term: פָּטוּר מִדִּינֵי אָדָם וְחַיָּיב בְּדִינֵי שָׁמַיִם
keyTerms.meaning: Exempt in human court, but liable in the laws of Heaven

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never says outright that produce makes you liable. רב ששת reads that into it: if the ברייתא mentions poison specifically, then produce must be different.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: I say,
that while dozing and lying down
phrases.notes: A polite way of saying רב's ruling was not carefully thought through.

phrases.english: Rav said this ruling.
For it is taught: One who places poison
before his fellow's animal
is exempt according to human laws,
but liable according to the laws of Heaven.

phrases.aramaic: סַם הַמָּוֶת הוּא דְּלָא עֲבִידָא דְּאָכְלָה;
phrases.english: It is poison, which an animal does not usually eat, that gets this ruling;
but produce, which an animal usually eats,
makes him liable according to human laws too!
But why? It should not have eaten!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: אָמֵינָא, כִּי נָיֵים וְשָׁכֵיב רַב אֲמַר לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning given in Step 13 for רב's exemption.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the produce owner is exempt when the animal eats the produce and is hurt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא limits the exemption to poison, which implies that edible produce brings liability in human court. That contradicts the 'it should not have eaten' reasoning.

steps.title: Produce is exempt too; the ברייתא's lesson is about Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The answer: produce is also exempt in human court. The ברייתא mentions poison to teach that even with poison, which animals do not usually eat, there is still liability in Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: The same is true even for produce. He is also exempt in human court. The ברייתא is teaching us that even poison, which an animal does not usually eat, still makes him liable in the laws of Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. It explains that the ברייתא chose poison for a different reason, not to set it apart from produce in human court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת's inference assumed that the poison case was about the human-court exemption. The answer flips the focus: the new point is the liability in Heaven. One might think there is no blame at all when the animal is not expected to eat the item, and the ברייתא teaches that there is still blame in Heaven. So nothing in the ברייתא contradicts רב.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us

phrases.english: They said: The same is true even for produce
he is also exempt according to human laws;
and this is what it teaches us:
that even poison too,
which an animal does not usually eat,
makes him liable according to the laws of Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's challenge by changing which part of the ברייתא carries the main lesson.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא mentions poison to show that only poison is exempt in human court.
steps.terutzMaskana: Produce is also exempt in human court. Poison is mentioned to teach that liability in Heaven applies even to it.

steps.title: The 'poison' is a plant that looks like food
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the ברייתא's poison is אפרזתא, a poisonous plant that animals eat like food. So it is the same as produce, and both are exempt in human court.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: the poison here is also something like אפרזתא, which counts as produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different defense of רב. It says the ברייתא's 'poison' is itself a kind of food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת's inference depended on poison being something animals do not eat. If the poison is אפרזתא, an edible-looking plant, then the ברייתא's exemption in human court is about food. That actually matches רב's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces a second answer
A poisonous plant that animals eat like normal food

steps.whyThisMatters: In this reading, the ברייתא no longer challenges רב. It directly backs up רב's ruling that a person is exempt in human court for harmful food an animal chose to eat.

phrases.english: And if you want, say: the poison too
is a case of afrazta, which counts as produce.
phrases.notes: A plant that looks like normal animal food but is poisonous, so the animal eats it like any produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, independent answer to רב ששת's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Poison' means something animals do not eat.
steps.terutzMaskana: The poison is אפרזתא, which animals do eat. So the exemption in human court applies to edible items, just as רב said.

steps.title: A challenge from the woman grinding wheat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a woman came in without permission to grind wheat. If the homeowner's animal ate her wheat, he is exempt. If the animal was hurt, she is liable. Why? The animal should not have eaten!
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: A woman came in to grind wheat at a homeowner's house without permission, and the homeowner's animal ate the wheat. He is exempt. If the animal was hurt, she is liable. But why? Let us say: the animal should not have eaten it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that seems to go directly against רב. Here the owner of the food is liable when the animal eats it and gets hurt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case matches רב's case closely. Food was placed where it did not belong, an animal ate it, and the animal was hurt. Yet the ברייתא makes the woman liable, which goes against רב's reasoning that the animal is to blame for eating.

keyTerms.meaning: They raised an objection: a challenge from a תנאי source

phrases.english: They raised an objection: A woman who entered
to grind wheat at a homeowner's place
without permission,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲכָלָתַן בְּהֶמְתּוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and the homeowner's animal ate them: he is exempt.
If it was hurt, she is liable.
phrases.notes: It was hurt means the animal; she means the woman.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַמַּאי? נֵימָא: הֲוָה לַהּ שֶׁלֹּא תֹּאכַל!
phrases.english: But why? Let us say: it should not have eaten!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רב from the poison ברייתא, the גמרא raises a new and more direct challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's exemption when an animal eats produce and is hurt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא makes the woman liable when the animal ate her wheat and was hurt. That directly goes against 'it should not have eaten.'

steps.title: The woman's case is about slipping, just like the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer the challenge from the woman grinding wheat. Just as we explained the משנה as a case where the animal slipped on the produce, the ברייתא can be explained the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: Is this ברייתא any stronger than our משנה, which we already explained as a case where the animal slipped on the produce?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 17. In the ברייתא, the homeowner's animal was hurt by slipping on the woman's wheat, not by eating it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed the animal was hurt from eating, and that clashes with רב's 'it should not have eaten.' But if the animal slipped, eating has nothing to do with it, so the woman is liable for a normal obstacle she created. We already used this exact answer for the משנה, so it works for the ברייתא too.

keyTerms.meaning: They said; the Sages in the study hall answer
We established it as; we explained the case as

phrases.english: They said: And is it any better than our משנה
phrases.notes: He means: is this ברייתא any harder to explain than our משנה?

phrases.english: which we explained as where it slipped on them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (slipping rather than eating), by comparison to the earlier explanation of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The animal in the ברייתא was hurt by eating the wheat, which goes against 'it should not have eaten.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The animal was hurt by slipping on the wheat, so the woman is liable, and רב's rule about eating is untouched.

steps.title: Why was the challenge even asked?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא wonders why anyone raised the woman's case as a challenge at all, since the slipping answer was already known from the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the one who raised this challenge, why did he raise it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a side question about the challenger. If the answer was this obvious, what was he thinking? This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A challenge should not be raised if a ready answer already exists. So the גמרא looks for a reason the challenger thought the ברייתא was different from the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: He raises it (as a difficulty); he asks it

phrases.english: And the one who asked it, why did he ask it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reasoning of the challenger in Step 17, given the easy answer in Step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What did the challenger see in the ברייתא that made him think the slipping answer would not work?

steps.title: The missing word 'by them'
steps.stepSummary: The challenger noticed a wording difference. The משנה says 'hurt by them,' which fits slipping on them. The ברייתא just says 'hurt,' which sounds like it was hurt from eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would say to you: In the משנה it makes sense. It says 'if it was hurt by them,' so it means the animal slipped on them. But here the ברייתא says only 'if it was hurt' and not 'by them.' So it must be talking about eating.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the challenger's thinking. It all comes down to whether the word בהן ('by them') appears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Hurt by them' points to the produce itself as an obstacle, which means slipping. Without בהן, and right after the line about the animal eating the wheat, the injury sounds like it came from the eating. That is why the challenger thought the slipping answer would not work for the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (in one case, but not the other)

phrases.english: He would say to you: It makes sense in the משנה,
since it teaches 'if it was hurt by them'
that is where it slipped on them;
but here, it teaches 'if it was hurt'
and does not teach 'by them'
so it is eating that it is teaching.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The challenger noticed that the ברייתא leaves out the word בהן, so he read its 'hurt' as hurt from eating.

steps.title: The other side: the wording makes no difference
steps.stepSummary: The one who gave the slipping answer says the missing word 'by them' changes nothing. The ברייתא can also be about slipping.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one would say to you: There is no difference.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answerer's reply. Whether or not it says 'by them,' the injury can still be from slipping.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenger built his case on one missing word. The answerer does not think that word matters, so the slipping answer stands for the ברייתא just as it did for the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: The other one (here, the one who answered)

steps.whatToRemember: The woman's case does not disprove רב: the animal was hurt by slipping on the wheat, not by eating it. The missing word בהן does not change that.

phrases.english: And the other one would say to you:
There is no difference.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the wording distinction raised in Step 20 and keeps the answer of Step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that leaving out בהן means the injury came from eating.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Plain 'hurt' can mean slipping just as well as 'hurt by them.'

steps.title: An ox eats wheat in a courtyard and dies
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: an ox entered a courtyard, ate wheat, got sick and died. If it came in without permission, the courtyard owner is exempt. If it came in with permission, he is liable. Why? The ox should not have eaten!
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone brought his ox into a homeowner's courtyard without permission, and it ate wheat, got diarrhea and died, the homeowner is exempt. If he brought it in with permission, the courtyard owner is liable. But why? It should not have eaten!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to challenge רב. Here the ox clearly died from eating, and still the courtyard owner pays when the ox was there with permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slipping answer cannot work this time, because the ברייתא says outright that the ox ate the wheat and died from it. רב's rule 'it should not have eaten' would put the blame on the ox. Yet the ברייתא makes the courtyard owner pay, so it seems to argue with רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear; introduces a source as a proof or challenge
Got diarrhea; became sick in the stomach
It should not have eaten (רב's reasoning)

steps.confusionAlert: Here the courtyard owner is the one who might pay, and the ox is the one that got hurt. Keep track of whose animal ate whose wheat.

phrases.english: Come and hear: If one brought his ox
into a homeowner's courtyard without permission,
and it ate wheat, got diarrhea and died, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the homeowner. The ox ate the homeowner's wheat.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם הִכְנִיס בִּרְשׁוּת – בַּעַל הֶחָצֵר חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: But if he brought it in with permission, the owner of the courtyard is liable.
But why? It should not have eaten!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הִכְנִיס שׁוֹרוֹ לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the woman's case is answered, a new ברייתא is brought against רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that an animal's owner cannot claim for harm from eating, because 'it should not have eaten.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ox was clearly harmed by eating, so the slipping answer cannot help. Still, the courtyard owner is liable when the ox entered with permission. That contradicts 'it should not have eaten.'

steps.title: Permission means he accepted guarding the ox
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the ברייתא's case is different, because there the ox came in with permission. Giving permission means the courtyard owner accepted the job of guarding the ox, so he is liable even if the ox strangled itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Are you comparing a case with permission to a case without permission? With permission, the courtyard owner accepted guarding the ox, and he is liable even if it strangled itself.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge from Step 22. He says the argument 'the ox should not have eaten' only works when the ox came in without permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenger treated the 'with permission' case like the 'without permission' case. רבא says they are not the same: once the owner gave permission, he took on the job of guarding the ox. Because of that, he is liable no matter how the ox got hurt, even if it was its own fault.

keyTerms.meaning: You are throwing (one case against another), meaning you are raising a contradiction
Guarding, being responsible for keeping something safe

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read 'even if it strangled itself' as saying the courtyard owner caused the harm. The point is that once he accepted guarding, he is liable even for harm the ox did to itself.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Are you throwing "with permission" against "without permission"?
With permission, he took upon himself guarding his ox,
phrases.notes: "He" is the courtyard owner, and "his ox" means the other man's ox.

phrases.english: and even if it strangled itself, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 22
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between cases (with permission versus without permission)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'ox should not have eaten' argument should exempt the courtyard owner in every case.
steps.terutzMaskana: When permission is given, the courtyard owner accepts guarding the ox and is liable even for harm it does to itself.

steps.title: How far does accepting guarding go?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly a courtyard owner accepts when he takes on guarding. Is it only guarding against damage from himself, or also against damage that comes from outside?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: where he accepted guarding, what is the law? Did he accept only guarding against damage from himself, or perhaps even guarding against damage from the outside world?
steps.whatsHappening: Building on רבא's idea, the גמרא raises a new question: what is included when someone accepts guarding?
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two choices. Either he only promised that he and his own things would not cause harm, or he promised to protect the items from any harm at all, even from outsiders. The answer decides whether he pays when something from outside does the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the חכמים)
Of himself, meaning damage coming from himself and his own things
Of the world, meaning damage coming from the outside

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the limit of a courtyard owner's responsibility once he lets things into his property.

phrases.english: A question was asked to them:
Where he took upon himself guarding, what is the law?
phrases.notes: "He" is the courtyard owner who gave permission.

phrases.english: Was it only guarding against himself that he accepted,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא אֲפִילּוּ נְטִירוּתָא דְּעָלְמָא קַבֵּיל עֲלֵיהּ?
phrases.english: or perhaps he accepted even guarding against the outside world?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question that builds on רבא's idea of accepting guarding
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether accepting guarding covers only damage from the courtyard owner himself, or also damage from outside sources

steps.title: Trying to prove it from an outside ox eating produce
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: produce was brought into a courtyard and an ox from elsewhere ate it. Without permission, exempt. With permission, liable. The גמרא suggests this refers to the courtyard owner, which would mean he accepted guarding even against outside damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear what רב יהודה בר סימון taught in the נזיקין of the school of קרנא: If someone brought his produce into a homeowner's courtyard without permission, and an ox came from elsewhere and ate it, exempt. If he brought it in with permission, liable. Who is exempt and who is liable? Isn't it the courtyard owner who is exempt, and the courtyard owner who is liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the question from Step 24 using a ברייתא about an outside ox eating produce in a courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The damage here comes from outside: an ox that does not belong to the courtyard owner. If the courtyard owner is liable when he gave permission, then his acceptance of guarding must include damage from the outside world. That would answer the question with the second choice.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, an attempt to bring a proof
The אמורא who taught this ברייתא
The collection of teachings about damages from the school of קרנא

phrases.english: Come and hear,
that Rav Yehuda bar Simon taught
in the Nezikin of the school of Karna:

phrases.aramaic: הִכְנִיס פֵּירוֹתָיו לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת,
phrases.english: If he brought his produce into a homeowner's courtyard without permission,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא שׁוֹר מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר וַאֲכָלָן – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox came from somewhere else and ate it, he is exempt.
But if he brought it in with permission, he is liable.
Who is exempt and who is liable?
Is it not that the courtyard owner is exempt,
and the courtyard owner is liable?
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the words in square brackets. They finish the question so it matches the first half.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּתָנֵי רַב יְהוּדָה בַּר סִימוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question in Step 24
steps.raayaObject: That accepting guarding includes protecting against damage from outside
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רב יהודה בר סימון from נזיקין דבי קרנא, read as referring to the courtyard owner

steps.title: No, the ruling is about the ox's owner
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The ברייתא can be read as talking about the owner of the ox that ate the produce, not the courtyard owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: No. It is the ox's owner who is exempt, and the ox's owner who is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from Step 25 by reading the ברייתא as talking about a different person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא's 'exempt' and 'liable' refer to the owner of the ox, then it tells us nothing about what the courtyard owner accepted. So the question from Step 24 is still not answered by this source.

keyTerms.meaning: They said, introducing an answer or rejection

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not answer the question from Step 24. It only shows that this ברייתא cannot prove either side.

phrases.english: They said: No;
the ox's owner is exempt,
and the ox's owner is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 25
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the attempted proof only, not the question itself
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the ברייתא refers to the courtyard owner, but it can refer to the ox's owner instead.

steps.title: Testing the idea that the ברייתא means the owner of the ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a challenge to the rejection in step 26. It begins: 'But if the ברייתא is talking about the owner of the ox,' and the question itself continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the ברייתא is talking about the owner of the ox,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a question against the rejection in step 26, which said the ברייתא is talking about the owner of the ox. These words only open the challenge. The actual problem is stated on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 saved the original question by moving the ברייתא's ruling from the courtyard owner to the ox's owner. Now the גמרא checks whether that reading really fits the ברייתא's rulings, 'without permission, exempt' and 'with permission, liable.' If those rulings do not make sense for the ox's owner, the rejection falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And if / but if. It introduces a possibility the גמרא is about to test.
The owner of the ox. Here it means the owner of the outside ox that ate the produce.

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new idea of its own. It picks up the suggestion from step 26 so the גמרא can challenge it. The problem itself comes at the start of the next amud.

phrases.english: But if it is the owner of the ox,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge to the rejection in step 26 by testing whether the ברייתא can really be read as talking about the owner of the ox.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading from step 26 that the ברייתא refers to the owner of the ox that ate the produce.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The setup suggests that the ברייתא's rulings ('without permission, exempt; with permission, liable') may not fit the owner of the ox. The full challenge is stated in the following text.
